ideas.title: Hexfall Kingdoms
ideas.concept: A 2-4 player hex tile-laying kingdom builder where every resource pip you harvest is drawn from a shared, finite bank that runs dry as the game goes on. Each turn you reveal and place a terrain hex to expand your kingdom, then race to harvest maturing resource pips off tiles before the bank's supply of that color is gone forever, turning unharvested tiles barren. A turn feels like a tight expand-or-harvest decision: grab now, or build toward a bigger future combo and risk the well running dry.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'hex tile kingdom building board game decaying resource dial mechanic' and 'Kingdomino BoardGameGeek' — results returned Kingdomino (domino-draft scoring, no resource pool), Kingdom Builder (card-driven placement, no scarcity economy) and Tiny Kingdom (combo-chain scoring, no shared depleting bank). None of the surveyed hex/kingdom tile-layers use a shared physical bank of resource pips that permanently depletes by color and converts unharvested tiles to zero-value 'barren' status. That specific scarcity-economy layered on hex kingdom-building is the unclaimed combination this design occupies; claim is scoped to this exact combination, not to tile-laying generally.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+, 45-60 min. SETUP: Each player takes a 9cm capital hex tile as the start of their personal kingdom (tiles are not shared — each player builds their own kingdom in their own tableau area). Shuffle the 48 terrain hexes face-down into a single stack. Fill the central bank tray with all 60 resource pips (12 each of 5 colors) in their labeled wells. TURN (clockwise): (1) Reveal the top terrain hex and place it touching at least one edge of your existing kingdom. If the tile has molded dimples, fill each with a pip of the matching color taken from the bank — if that color's well is empty, the dimple stays permanently empty (the tile scores 0 for that dimple all game). (2) Optional harvest: if a tile in your kingdom that was placed on an earlier turn (not this turn) is touching 2+ of your tiles that still hold a pip of the same color, you may remove one such pip and add it to your personal supply tray — this pip is now permanently yours and is removed from the board (it does not return to the bank). (3) Optional claim: if a face-up kingdom order tile (from a row of 4, refilled from a shuffled stack of 16) shows an icon you meet (e.g. 'hold 3+ pips of one color'), take it into your score pile. CONTINUE until the terrain stack is exhausted, then finish the current round so all players get equal turns. SCORING: 1 point per pip in your personal supply, plus the engraved point value (2-5) of each kingdom order tile you claimed. Highest total wins; ties split by most unclaimed order-tile requirements still met.
ideas.components: 48 hex terrain tiles (5 color-coded terrain types), PETG, 4.5cm flat-to-flat x 4mm thick, each with 0-2 molded dimples (3mm dia x 2mm deep); 60 resource pip tokens (5 colors x 12), PLA, cone shape 8mm base x 10mm tall; 1 central bank tray, PETG, 15x10x1cm with 5 labeled wells (icon molded, 12-pip capacity each); 4 capital hex tiles (one per player color), PLA, 9cm flat-to-flat x 5mm; 16 kingdom order tiles, PLA, 4x4cm x 3mm, engraved icon + point value; 4 player supply trays, PETG, 10x6x1.5cm; 1 turn-order d4 die, PLA, 1.5cm; 1 storage box with fitted hex compartments, PETG, 22x18x6cm.
ideas.demand_case: Tile-laying kingdom-builders are one of the strongest-selling family board game subgenres — Kingdomino (Blue Orange, hex/domino kingdom building) won the 2017 Spiel des Jahres, the industry's top family-game award, and spawned multiple spin-offs (Queendomino, Kingdomino Origins, Age of Giants) confirming sustained repeat demand for this exact mechanic family. Target audience: family game night and casual strategy gamers, ages 10+, who already own or want a Kingdomino/Kingdom Builder-adjacent game.
ideas.fun_case: The core tension each turn is expand-vs-harvest under a visibly shrinking shared resource — you can see the bank wells emptying, which creates the same 'grab it before it's gone' urgency that makes worker-placement and scarcity-bank games (e.g. Great Western Trail's limited buildings, Puerto Rico's finite goods) replayable. Layered onto a 45-60 min tile-laying frame validated by Kingdomino's mainstream success, this gives light-medium strategy gamers a genuine planning puzzle without pushing complexity into heavy-euro territory.
ideas.producibility_notes: 12 unique part types, ~180 total pieces, no moving joints anywhere in the design — dimples are static sockets, not hinges or dials, so tolerance risk is low (a 3mm dimple needs only enough clearance for an 8mm pip base to rest in, not to snap-fit). The bank tray's 5 wells are the only feature needing dimensional care (must visibly show fill level for the 'shrinking supply' tension to read at the table) but require no moving parts. Riskiest feature is simply keeping the 48 terrain hex edges dimensionally consistent enough to tile flush against each other at scale — a solved problem in hex-tile FDM printing.
ideas.prompt: Product photography of a finished tabletop board game called Hexfall Kingdoms: a low box lid resting open beside an in-progress hex tile kingdom made of matte 3D-printed hexagonal tiles in five terrain colors (forest green, stone grey, wheat gold, river blue, desert tan) fitted edge to edge into an organic sprawling cluster on a wooden tabletop, small cone-shaped translucent resin pips of matching colors nestled in shallow tile dimples, a rectangular central bank tray with five labeled wells partially emptied of colored pips sitting beside the kingdom, four small engraved square order tiles and a tiny d4 die in the foreground, warm studio lighting, shallow depth of field, overhead-angled product shot.

ideas.title: Gearlock Derby
ideas.concept: A 2-4 player mechanical racing game where you draft and physically mesh interlocking gear tiles onto a circuit board to build a working drivetrain, then crank a central engine each round to watch your racers get carried forward by the gears they're standing on. Every turn is a spatial puzzle of where to bolt the next gear so it both meshes into the existing train and gives your own racer the best push, while rivals fight to hijack the chain for themselves.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'mechanical gear train racing board game 3d printed gears' — found Gearz (2-player abstract clone of the 1975 game 'The Power Game': turn one gear each turn trying to spin the opponent's master gear, no racing or track) and Gear Towers (territory-control game where rotating gears change which towers connect, no racer movement or crank-propulsion). Neither existing design uses a physically cranked drive train to propel racer pawns along a numbered track; that combination — drafted meshing gears as a transmission that mechanically moves pawns when a shared crank is turned — is not present in either cited product, so the claim is scoped to this exact race-by-transmission mechanism.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+, 30-45 min. SETUP: Place the circuit board (a 40-space numbered loop track with 24 fixed axle posts) on the table. Seat the drive crank gear on the central 'engine' axle post. Shuffle the 40 gear tiles face-down and reveal 6 into the draft rack. Each player places their racer pawn onto the gear tile seated at the axle post nearest the engine (start with that first gear pre-placed and meshed to the engine). TURN (clockwise), each player rolls the d6 for action points (result 2-4), then spends them 1-for-1 on any combination of: draft a gear tile from the rack to your player mat (rack refills from the face-down stack); place a gear tile from your mat onto any empty axle post that is close enough to touch teeth with an existing meshed gear in the train (the axle grid only allows valid same-or-adjacent-size meshes, enforced physically by post spacing); or move your racer pawn to sit on any other gear tile currently in the connected train. END OF ROUND: after every player has acted once, the starting player turns the drive crank one full rotation. Every gear tile connected via an unbroken mesh chain back to the drive gear causes any racer pawn seated on it to move forward along the track by that gear's printed rotation value (Small gear = 2 spaces, Medium = 1 space, Large = 1 space). WIN: the first racer to complete the 40-space loop and return to the engine space wins immediately.
ideas.components: 1 circuit board, PETG, 30x30cm, printed with a 40-space numbered loop track and 24 fixed axle posts (6mm dia); 40 gear tiles across 3 sizes (Small 8-tooth ~3cm dia x14, Medium 12-tooth ~4.5cm dia x13, Large 16-tooth ~6cm dia x13), PETG, each with a 6.3mm center bore (0.3mm clearance over axle posts for free rotation and tooth meshing); 1 drive crank gear with integrated hand-turnable knob, PLA, 8cm dia, keyed to the fixed engine axle; 4 racer pawns, PLA, 3cm each with a flat 4mm peg base that seats into a gear tile's tooth notch; 1 gear-draft display rack, PETG, holds 6 face-up tiles; 4 player mats with small gear-holding trays, PETG; 1 d6 die, PLA; storage box with gear-shaped tray inserts, PETG.
ideas.demand_case: Board Games with Gears on the Board is an active, curated BGG geeklist and dedicated hobbyist STL projects (Gearz, Gear Towers, Gear game board on Cults3D/Printables) show a standing maker/hobbyist appetite for functional interlocking-gear mechanisms in games, and family racing games with a strong physical gimmick (Downforce, Formula D) are an established mid-weight family/gamer-crossover category. Target audience: family/gateway gamers and mechanism-curious hobbyists, ages 10+, who want a race game with a tactile, visibly-moving centerpiece.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is a spatial trade-off — do you extend the train toward your own racer's gear, or place a gear that blocks a rival's connection, knowing every placement is permanent and public. That build-the-machine-together-but-race-apart tension mirrors what makes Downforce's shared-track betting and Formula D's physical movement engaging, but adds a genuinely new layer: your progress depends on a mechanism you and your opponents jointly constructed, so sabotage-via-placement is a constant live option, not just a card effect.
ideas.producibility_notes: 40 gear tiles is the highest single-part-type count in this set and all 40 share the same repeated risky feature: a center bore meshing over a fixed axle post with a 0.3mm clearance tolerance. This is a static resting fit (gear drops onto a post and rests there, no snap or press-fit), not a hinge or friction joint, which keeps per-instance risk low even at this count — the same passive-mesh approach is already demonstrated working in hobbyist prints like Gearz and Gear Towers per search. The one component needing tighter tolerance control is the axle-post grid spacing on the circuit board itself, since it must guarantee valid tooth meshes only at intended size-pairings; this is a single fixed print (not repeated per-unit) so the risk is contained to getting one master file right.
ideas.prompt: Product photography of a finished tabletop board game called Gearlock Derby: a square matte-black plastic circuit board printed with a numbered spiral racetrack lies on a wooden table, dozens of interlocking 3D-printed gears in three sizes (small orange, medium teal, large yellow) meshed together in a winding chain across the board with a larger central hand-crank gear in brushed silver-grey at the middle, four small colorful racer pawns perched on different gears along the chain, a stack of extra gear tiles and a six-sided die in the foreground, dramatic side lighting emphasizing the gear teeth, overhead three-quarter product shot.

ideas.title: Fortress Echo
ideas.concept: A 2-player hidden-fortress duel where you're not just guessing a grid coordinate, you're guessing which of three physical elevation levels an enemy structure occupies. Every shot means rotating your trajectory dial to low, mid, or high before calling a square, and a wrong-elevation hit still tells your opponent something — it echoes back that a structure is there, just not where you aimed.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: Battleship's hidden-grid call-and-reveal shooting. Searched 'Battleship hidden fortress elevation arc trajectory board game' and found only classic Battleship (flat 2D grid, one shot = one coordinate, binary hit/miss/sunk) and a hexagonal-grid Battleship variant with islands — no result adds a third hidden dimension (elevation level) that must be matched in addition to the coordinate, and no result has a 'near-miss echo' feedback state distinct from a clean miss. The specific rule change here — shots require BOTH a coordinate AND a declared elevation, with a partial-info 'echo' result when the coordinate is right but elevation is wrong — is not present in the cited base game or its found variants.
ideas.rules: 2 players, ages 10+, 30 min. SETUP: Each player sets up their opaque privacy screen and 8x8 socket grid board. Behind the screen, secretly place your 5 fortress ships (lengths 2, 2, 3, 4, 5 in grid cells, oriented horizontally or vertically as in classic Battleship) by inserting stacking peg segments into the sockets that ship occupies; choose one elevation level (Ground/Mid/High) for each entire ship and mark it by inserting a colored elevation pip at the ship's first cell (visible only to you, tracked on your own reference). Each player also takes 1 siege token. TURN (alternating): the active player announces a grid coordinate and rotates their own trajectory selector disc to declare an elevation (Low/Mid/High) for this shot. The defending player checks their board: if a ship occupies that exact cell at that exact elevation, announce 'HIT' — attacker places a red peg on their tracking board at that cell, defender marks it on their own board too. If a ship occupies that cell but at a DIFFERENT elevation, announce 'ECHO' — attacker places a special echo peg there (marks 'something is here, wrong level'). If no ship occupies that cell at any elevation, announce 'MISS' — attacker places a white peg. Once per game, either player may spend their siege token to check all 3 elevations at one coordinate simultaneously as their turn's shot (guaranteed to reveal the true state of that cell at all levels). A ship is sunk once every one of its cells has been hit at its correct elevation; the defender must announce 'SUNK' and reveal which ship. WIN: first player to sink all 5 enemy ships wins.
ideas.components: 2 opaque privacy screens, PETG, 25x15cm folding standing panels; 2 base grid boards (8x8 socket grid, 8mm sockets), PETG, 20x20cm; 5 fortress ships per player (10 total; lengths 2,2,3,4,5 in cells), PLA bars 2cm x (length x2cm) x 1cm, each with one insertable colored elevation pip (1cm) marking Ground/Mid/High; 2 tracking boards (8x8 hole grid for the attacker's own shot record), PETG, 20x20cm; 128 peg markers total (64 red hit pegs, 64 white miss pegs), PLA, 4mm; 32 echo pegs (16 per player, distinct color/shape), PLA, 4mm; 2 trajectory selector discs, PETG, 6cm dia rotating disc with 3 marked zones on a center press-fit pivot pin; 4 siege tokens (2 per player), PLA, small triangular chips; storage box with peg-tray compartments, PETG.
ideas.demand_case: Battleship is one of the best-known deduction games in the world with a permanent BGG presence and continuous retail life (Hasbro classic edition, hex variant, card game spin-off, mobile/app ports per search), demonstrating an enormous, durable mainstream audience for grid-based hidden-placement deduction. Target audience: families and casual 2-player game nights, ages 10+, who already know Battleship's rules and want a deeper deduction layer without learning a new genre.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is no longer just 'where do I shoot' but 'where AND at what height,' effectively doubling the deduction space per shot — an echo result is genuinely informative (narrows the ship to a coordinate, forces the defender to worry it'll be found on the next elevation guess) without being a full hit, which creates the same tense probability-tracking that makes Battleship's simple deduction loop replayable, just with one more axis of bluffing (ships can be placed at Low or High specifically to bait opponents into wasting siege tokens). 30-minute 2-player playtime matches the audience's existing Battleship session length exactly.
ideas.producibility_notes: 10 core part types. The trajectory selector disc's center press-fit pivot pin is the only true moving-joint risk in the design, but it appears in only 2 instances (one per player), keeping repeated-joint risk low per the general rule that risk compounds with count, not with the joint type itself. The 8x8 socket grids (128 total sockets across 2 boards) are static holes, not moving parts, so tolerance only needs to fit a 4mm peg with light friction — a well-solved FDM feature. The riskiest tolerance is the stacking peg elevation markers seating firmly enough in ship-piece slots that they don't fall out during screened setup handling, which should use a simple friction-fit peg, not a snap.
ideas.prompt: Product photography of a finished tabletop board game called Fortress Echo: two matching 3D-printed square grid boards face each other on a dark wooden table, each behind a tall folding opaque privacy screen printed with a stylized fortress silhouette, small colorful plastic ship-bar pieces with tiny colored elevation pegs visible on one open board, a round rotating trajectory selector dial with three colored zones sitting beside each board, red and white peg markers scattered in labeled tracking grids, dramatic overhead studio lighting, symmetrical two-player product composition.

ideas.title: Monsoon Route
ideas.concept: A 2-4 player nautical pickup-and-deliver game where the sea itself doesn't exist until you sail into it — you reveal and snap new hex tiles into place as your ship approaches the edge of the known map, while a shared rotating wind compass silently helps or hinders everyone's movement each round. A turn feels like planning three moves ahead against a map and a wind direction that both keep changing under you.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'pickup and deliver desert caravan dice board game water resource management' and found Caravan (Rio Grande Games, fixed desert-camel board, theft mechanic, no modular map or shared movement modifier) and Through the Desert (fixed board, camel-chain area-majority scoring, no delivery orders or expanding map). Neither uses a dynamically revealed/expanding modular board combined with a shared rotating wind-direction modifier that changes every player's movement identically each round. That specific combination — board unknown until explored plus a shared global movement constraint that shifts on a schedule — is not present in either cited comparable, so the claim is scoped to this combination rather than to pickup-and-deliver generally.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+, 45 min. SETUP: Place the home port hex at the table center; shuffle the 36 sea/island hexes face-down into a stack beside it. Each player takes a ship pawn starting at the home port, an empty cargo rack, and 2 face-up delivery order chips (drawn from a shuffled stack of 18, with 6 more revealed in a shared face-up row). TURN (clockwise): (1) Roll the d6 for movement points. (2) The active player rotates the monsoon compass dial (only once, at the very start of their own turn) to set this round's shared wind direction, visible to all. (3) Move your ship up to your movement points across connected hexes, one hex per point; if you move WITH the wind arrow's direction, add +1 free movement point that step; if AGAINST it, that step costs +1 extra point (minimum net 1 point spent per hex). If your movement path would cross the edge of the currently placed board, instead reveal and place the top hex from the stack there before continuing (reef hazard tiles may never be placed touching another reef hazard tile — reshuffle and redraw if this would occur). (4) At any port hex you occupy, load goods cubes matching that port's icon (up to your rack's 4-cube capacity) or, if you're carrying goods matching an order chip's destination icon and you're at that destination port, unload them to fulfill the order: score its printed reward value (2-6), discard the chip, and draw a new order into your hand from the shared row. GAME END: when the sea hex stack is exhausted and the current round finishes, the game ends. WIN: highest total reward value scored wins; ties broken by most goods cubes still in cargo.
ideas.components: 1 home port starting hex, PETG, 8cm flat-to-flat x 4mm; 36 sea/island/reef hexes, PETG, 8cm flat-to-flat x 4mm with 2mm interlocking edge tabs/notches; 1 monsoon compass dial, PETG, 10cm dia rotating disc with 6 wind arrows on a center press-fit pivot pin; 4 ship pawns, PLA, 3cm boat-shaped miniatures, one per player color; 30 goods cubes (5 types x 6), PLA, 1cm cubes; 4 player cargo racks, PETG, small 4-slot trays; 4 player order-chip holders, PETG; 18 delivery order chips, PLA, 3x3cm engraved with origin/destination icons and reward value; 1 d6 movement die, PLA; storage box, PETG.
ideas.demand_case: Pickup-and-deliver is an established, actively curated BGG mechanic category (per boardgame.tips 'best games with pickup and deliver' roundup and multiple shipped comparables — Caravan, Through the Desert, Ticket to Ride's route-building lineage) with a proven mid-weight family/hobbyist crossover audience. Target audience: family and light-strategy gamers, ages 10+, who enjoy route-planning games like Ticket to Ride or Through the Desert and want a nautical theme with a growing, unpredictable map.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is route planning under two simultaneously moving targets — the map itself is incomplete (you don't know what's past the edge until you commit movement to reveal it) and the wind direction changes every round, so a route that was efficient last round may now be penalized. This double-uncertainty is a genuine escalation of the route-optimization tension that makes Ticket to Ride and Through the Desert replayable, adding a push-your-luck exploration layer (do you commit to revealing new tiles or stick to the known, wind-favorable map) absent from either cited comparable.
ideas.producibility_notes: 38 hex tiles total is a large part count but each is a static interlocking piece (tab/notch edges, no moving mechanism) — the only true moving joint in the whole game is the single monsoon compass dial's center pivot pin, which appears in exactly 1 instance, the lowest-risk case for a repeated-joint concern. The riskiest tolerance is the hex edge tab/notch fit (2mm features) needing to interlock snugly enough to keep the modular board flat and stable as it grows to 30+ tiles, without being so tight that placement during play is fiddly — this should be validated with a single tab/notch prototype pair before scaling to all 37 edges.
ideas.prompt: Product photography of a finished tabletop board game called Monsoon Route: an irregular expanding cluster of 3D-printed ocean-blue and sandy-tan hexagonal tiles interlocked together on a wooden table depicting open sea, small palm-tree islands, and reef hazard tiles, four small painted boat-shaped pawns in red, yellow, green and blue positioned across the tiles, a circular wind-compass dial with painted arrows sitting to one side, small colorful cube tokens and engraved delivery chips scattered near a player tray, warm nautical lighting with a teal and sand color palette, overhead three-quarter product shot.

ideas.title: Chrono Loop
ideas.concept: A 2-4 player programmed-movement race where you secretly plan three moves at once, then watch chaos unfold as everyone reveals simultaneously — and if your pawn collides with another, you don't just stop, you get yanked backward to where you were two moves ago, as if the collision unwound time. Every round is a bet on where rivals will be, knowing a wrong guess costs you real ground.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'time loop puzzle race board game rewind mechanic' — every result was a video game (Braid, It Takes Two, Timelie) or general TV Tropes/listicle content; no shipped tabletop board game surfaced with a rewind-on-collision mechanic. Searched programmed-movement racing comparables (Roborally, Formula D) separately as the closest tabletop genre for demand evidence: those use simultaneous programmed movement but resolve collisions with simple blocking/damage, never a positional rewind to a tracked earlier position. The specific combination — simultaneous 3-step programmed movement plus a physical 'echo trail' marker system that sends colliding pawns back to their tracked position from 2 steps earlier — was not found in any searched tabletop product, so the claim is scoped to tabletop board games specifically, not video games broadly.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+, 30-40 min. SETUP: Place all racer pawns at space 0 on the 48-space spiral track (loop points marked every 8th space). Each player takes a 3-slot program tray with an opaque lid, and 6 movement tokens (two each valued 1, 2, 3). ROUND: (1) SECRETLY, each player places any 3 of their 6 movement tokens (repeats allowed) into their tray's slots A, B, C in the order they want them to resolve, then closes the lid. (2) All players open their lids simultaneously. (3) Resolve in three steps, A then B then C: for each step, in turn order, move each pawn forward by that step's token value; immediately before moving a pawn each step, drop an 'echo trail' marker at its current space (these mark that pawn's position history). If, at the end of any step, two or more pawns occupy the same space, every pawn in that collision is immediately moved backward to the space marked by its own echo trail marker from 2 steps earlier (using that pawn's own trail, not another's) and that marker is removed. If a pawn has fewer than 2 prior echo markers yet (early in the game), it instead returns to space 0. (4) After step C resolves, all spent movement tokens return to each player's hand for next round (tokens are never permanently lost). Landing exactly on a loop point space grants a free immediate repeat of that step's movement value. GAME END: the first pawn to reach or pass space 48 (the center Convergence space) at the end of any step wins immediately.
ideas.components: 1 spiral race track board, PETG, ~35cm dia, printed with 48 numbered spaces and loop-point markers every 8 spaces; 4 racer pawns, PLA, 3cm, one per color; 4 program trays (3-slot each with an opaque sliding lid), PETG, 8x4x1.5cm; 24 movement tokens (4 players x 6: two each of value 1/2/3), PLA, 1.5cm discs engraved with number; 60 echo trail markers (15 per player, flat 1cm discs in player color), PLA; storage box, PETG.
ideas.demand_case: Programmed simultaneous-movement racing is an established mid-weight mechanic with proven mainstream success (Roborally has sustained multiple editions since 1994; Formula D remains in print as a dice-and-planning racer), showing durable demand for the 'plan ahead, reveal, and hope you predicted rivals correctly' tension. Target audience: family and gateway-strategy gamers, ages 10+, who enjoy light-planning racers and want a shorter (30-40 min), lower-complexity alternative to Roborally's board-damage rules overhead.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is predictive bluffing under simultaneous reveal — you're not reacting to what opponents did, you're guessing what they WILL do and programming around it, the exact tension that makes Roborally and Formula D replayable session after session. The rewind-on-collision twist raises the stakes of that guess without adding rules overhead (no damage tracks or programming cards to shuffle), keeping session length and rules complexity appropriate for the stated family/gateway audience rather than Roborally's heavier hobbyist weight class.
ideas.producibility_notes: 11 part types, no complex rotating mechanisms anywhere in the design — the only moving feature is each program tray's sliding opaque lid (4 instances, one per player), which is a simple groove-slide, not a snap-hinge or friction pivot, so the repeated-feature risk is low and the joint type itself is inherently low-tolerance-sensitivity (a loose slide still functions as a cover). The highest part count is the 60 echo trail markers, but these are flat static discs with no fit tolerance at all. No feature in the entire component list is under 1mm.
ideas.prompt: Product photography of a finished tabletop board game called Chrono Loop: a circular 3D-printed spiral racetrack board with 48 numbered segments spiraling inward toward a glowing center space sits on a dark table, four small colorful pawn racers positioned at different points along the spiral trailing small flat disc markers behind them like a comet tail, four rectangular player program trays with sliding lids open beside the board showing engraved numbered tokens inside, a cool blue and violet sci-fi color palette with subtle glow accents, dramatic overhead lighting, product photo composition.

ideas.title: Aurora Peak
ideas.concept: A 2-4 player dexterity stacking game where you draft irregular rock pieces from a rotating carousel and balance them into your own mountain, racing to plant your climber pawn on top before a tremor roll shakes the table. Every turn is a gamble between grabbing a safe small rock or a big unstable one that scores more but might send your whole climb crashing down.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'dexterity stacking coral reef board game 3d printed pieces' and 'Junk Art dexterity stacking game abstract shapes drafting review' — found Junk Art (drafts objective cards specifying shape/color to build, scores 'fan' points for fulfilling venue conditions, wooden pieces) and Reef/Coral/Coral Gardens (card-driven reef piece selection, stacking up to a fixed height, scored by visibility from above, wooden pieces). None of these use a rotating physical draft carousel in place of card drafting, and none combine a shared 'tremor' collapse-check mechanic with a climbing-pawn summit objective that must survive a full opponent round to score. That specific combination is the unclaimed space this design occupies.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 8+, 25-35 min. SETUP: Place the rotating draft carousel at the table center loaded with 6 random rock pieces (drawn from the shuffled full 60-piece set) on its platforms; the remaining pieces form a face-down reserve stack beside it. Each player takes a base plate and a climber pawn. TURN: (1) Either rotate the carousel one position and take the newly-front piece, OR take the piece currently at the front position without rotating (your choice) — refill the vacated carousel slot from the reserve stack. (2) Place the drafted piece onto your own stack on your base plate; it must come to rest without you steadying it after release (resting on the base plate or on previously placed pieces is fine). If it falls off the base plate, discard it face-down back into the reserve pile (reshuffled in later) and your turn ends with no placement. (3) If your stack now stands 5 or more pieces tall, immediately roll the tremor die: on a 'tremor' result (2 of 6 faces), every player whose stack is 5+ tall must gently tap their own base plate once; any stack that topples loses all pieces above height 3 (those pieces return face-down to the reserve, reshuffled in) and that player's stack is rebuilt from height 3 up. (4) Instead of drafting, you may place your climber pawn balanced on top of your current stack to attempt a summit. If it remains balanced through every other player's next full turn without your stack toppling, plant a peak flag: score points equal to your stack's current height, remove the climber (the stack itself stays intact), and you may keep building toward a second summit later. GAME END: when the reserve stack and carousel are both empty. SCORING: sum of all points scored from planted peak flags, plus 1 bonus point per piece remaining in your stack. Highest total wins.
ideas.components: 4 personal base plates, PETG, 10cm dia round textured disc; 60 rock pieces across 4 tiers (Tier 1 small ~2cm x20, Tier 2 medium ~3cm x18, Tier 3 large ~4cm x14, Tier 4 summit-cap ~5cm x8), PLA, irregular asymmetric polyhedral shapes across 4-5 unique molds per tier, matte textured finish; 1 rotating draft carousel, PETG, 20cm dia turntable with 6 raised platforms on a center press-fit pivot; 4 climber pawns, PLA, 2cm humanoid minis, one per player color, flat friction-peg base; 1 tremor d6 die (4 'stable' faces, 2 'tremor' faces), PLA; 12 peak flag tokens (small flag-on-pole), PLA; storage box with tier-separated compartments, PETG.
ideas.demand_case: Dexterity stacking is a proven, actively growing mid-weight family category — Junk Art has sustained multiple printings and strong reviews across major board game press (RPGnet, Zatu, Board Game Quest, There Will Be Games per search), and the reef-stacking niche (Reef, Coral, Coral Gardens) demonstrates the same core mechanic supports several co-existing shipped products. Target audience: family game night and party-game groups, ages 8+, who enjoy tactile, physically tense games like Junk Art or Rhino Hero.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is risk-calibration under physical uncertainty — bigger pieces score more height but destabilize your stack faster, and the carousel forces you to commit to the piece currently in front of you rather than searching for a perfect one, which is exactly the constrained-choice-under-physical-risk tension that makes Junk Art's forced shape drafting and Rhino Hero's escalating tower both replayable. The added climbing-pawn summit objective gives a clear mid-game scoring checkpoint (unlike Junk Art's end-of-game-only fan scoring), which shortens the feedback loop for the stated family audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 8 part types, one true moving joint in the entire design: the draft carousel's center pivot, appearing in a single instance (lowest-risk case for a repeated-joint concern). The 60 rock pieces have zero fit-tolerance requirements since they rest freely rather than interlocking — their design risk is entirely in center-of-mass sculpting for satisfying-but-not-impossible balance, which is a CAD/playtesting concern rather than a printing-tolerance one. No feature anywhere in the bill is under 1mm.

ideas.title: Crystal Cavern
ideas.concept: A 2-4 player area-majority abstract game played on a board pre-molded with irregular fracture veins that carve it into oddly-shaped scoring regions, where a die roll each turn forces you to place whichever crystal color it shows — sometimes helping a rival's region, sometimes letting you strategically dilute one. A turn feels like tactical judo: you rarely get to place your own color freely, so you're constantly deciding whose region to help or wreck.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'crystal geode growth area scoring tile board game enclosed region' and found Geode (District 31: form a complete 4-tile circle of one color on an open grid, no fixed regions) and Gemstones (asymmetric connected-shard area control, penalizes disconnected pieces, no shared placement die or fixed board regions). Neither uses a board with a fixed, pre-molded irregular-region pattern (fracture veins baked into the physical board at manufacture, not formed by player placement) nor a shared color-forcing die that makes every player sometimes place a color that isn't their own. That specific combination — fixed fractured-region board plus forced-color placement — is the unclaimed space here.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+, 30-40 min. SETUP: Place the cavern board at the center (its surface is permanently molded with raised fracture veins dividing it into 24 irregular polygonal cells of varying size, each with 2-4 chip sockets and a molded numeral showing its score multiplier: 1x for small cells, 2x for large cells, 3x for 'resonance' cells that border 3+ other cells). Fill the shared bank with all 96 crystal chips (24 each of 4 colors). Assign each player one of the 4 colors as their scoring color (for 3 players, the 4th color is neutral and scores to nobody; for 2 players, 2 colors are neutral). TURN (clockwise): roll the vein d4 die to determine which color must be placed this turn. Take 1 chip of that color from the bank and place it into any empty socket that is adjacent to at least one already-filled socket (or anywhere if the board is currently empty). Play continues, looping through players, until the board's sockets are completely full. SCORING: for each of the 24 cells, whichever color has the most chips in that cell scores its owning player points equal to (chip count in that cell x that cell's printed multiplier); ties in a cell score to nobody. Sum all cells; highest total wins.
ideas.components: 1 cavern board, PETG (translucent tinted), 30x30cm, molded with 24 irregular fracture-divided cells (each with 2-4 sockets, 1.5cm dia) and a printed multiplier numeral per cell; 96 crystal chips (4 colors x 24), PLA translucent-look faceted gem shape, 1.5cm; 1 vein d4 die (4 crystal colors), PLA, 1.5cm; storage box, PETG.
ideas.demand_case: Area-majority abstract games with fixed boards are a proven, evergreen BGG category (Go, Blokus-family, and the crystal/gem-themed niche specifically shown active by Geode's Kickstarter run and Gemstones' 2023+ BGG listing per search), indicating steady standing demand for short, visually striking abstract area-control games. Target audience: abstract-strategy hobbyists and family game night groups, ages 10+, who enjoy short (30-40 min) tactile territory games like Blokus or Go variants.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is forced-color tactics — you rarely control which color you're placing, so the real decision is WHERE that forced color helps you least and hurts a rival most (or, when it's your own color, where it clinches a contested cell), a give-and-take tension distinct from the free-choice placement in Geode or Gemstones. This creates a shorter, sharper version of area-majority tension similar to what makes Blokus and Go's territory fights replayable, scaled down to a 30-40 min session appropriate for the stated family/hobbyist crossover audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: Only 4 part types in the entire bill and zero moving joints anywhere — the board is a single static molded piece and all other components are freely-resting chips and a die. The only manufacturing risk is ensuring the 24 irregular cell boundaries (fracture veins) are raised distinctly enough (recommend minimum 2mm ridge height) to be unambiguous during play, and that all ~80 total sockets across the board are dimensionally consistent enough to seat 1.5cm chips without excess play. No feature is under 1mm and no assembly/hardware is required.

ideas.title: Market Tides
ideas.concept: A 3-5 player blind-bid trading game where a rotating tide dial predictably cycles which goods type gets discounted each round, so savvy players hold back their coin for the exact moment their favorite goods swing cheap. Every round you slide a hidden peg to your secret bid, and the reveal is the tense part — did you time the tide right, or did everyone else see the same discount coming?
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: blind-bid auction games in the High Society / Ra tradition (simultaneous secret bidding, highest bid wins the lot). Searched 'blind bid auction board game rotating dial wind track' — found only general blind-bidding resources (BGDF forum threads, a BGG geeklist of blind bidding games, a generic 'board game dial' patent for attribute tracks unrelated to bidding) and no product combining a predictably-rotating shared price modifier with peg-based simultaneous bid reveal. High Society's value modifiers come from randomly drawn cards each round (unpredictable), not a dial players can see coming and plan multiple rounds ahead around; that predictable-rotation-plus-periodic-random-reset structure is the specific unclaimed mechanism here.
ideas.rules: 3-5 players, ages 12+, 30 min. SETUP: Shuffle the 20 goods lot tiles (5 types x 4, each with an engraved base value 2-9) face-down into a stack. Each player starts with coin tokens totaling 20 (e.g. one 10, two 5s). Set the tide dial's outer ring to any starting position. ROUND: (1) Reveal the top goods lot tile. (2) Check the tide dial: the outer ring shows a fixed multiplier (x0.5/x1/x1.5/x2) per goods type for this round (this ring's position is always visible in advance since it only rotates one wedge at the END of each round, letting players plan ahead); every 3rd round, additionally spin the inner ring at the start of that round for an extra random modifier layer. Compute this round's true bid ceiling reference: base value x current type multiplier (rounded to nearest whole number) — this is informational only, players may bid any amount up to their coin total regardless. (3) All players simultaneously set their bid board's slider to a secret amount (0 up to their full coin total) and close the flap. (4) All flaps open at once. The highest bidder pays their bid amount in coins to the shared bank and takes the goods lot tile (kept face-up as scored points, not spendable again); if there's a tie for highest, all tied bidders fail to acquire it and it is discarded from the game. (5) Rotate the tide dial's outer ring one wedge before the next round begins. GAME END: when the goods lot stack is exhausted. SCORING: sum of the printed base values of all goods lot tiles you won, plus 1 bonus point per 5 leftover coins (rounded down). Highest score wins.
ideas.components: 1 tide dial, PETG, 12cm dia, two concentric rotating rings (outer: 5 goods-type wedges with multiplier icons; inner: secondary random modifier wedges) on a center press-fit dual-axle; 20 goods lot tiles (5 types x 4), PLA, 4x4cm engraved with type icon and base value; 5 player bid boards, PETG, 10x6cm each with a slide-track peg (0-20 marked) and a hinged opaque cover flap; 60 coin tokens (denominations 1/5/10, ~20 each), PLA, 1.5-2.5cm engraved discs; 1 starting player marker, PLA; storage box, PETG.
ideas.demand_case: Blind-bidding is a well-established, actively curated BGG mechanic with a dedicated 'Top 10 Blind Bidding Games' video series (Tom Vasel/BGG) and multiple long-running comparables (High Society remains in print with a 2023 reprint, Ra is a recognized classic auction game) confirming durable hobbyist demand for the genre. Target audience: BGG light-to-mid-weight hobbyists and family groups who enjoy short (30 min) tense bidding games like High Society or For Sale.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is timing under partial predictability — because the outer dial rotates on a known schedule, you can plan several rounds ahead ('goods type C will be cheap in 2 rounds, I should hold back coin now'), a forward-planning layer that High Society's fully-random card reveals don't offer, while the periodic inner-ring spin every 3rd round reintroduces enough uncertainty to stop pure optimization. This gives the stated audience the same tense simultaneous-reveal thrill that makes High Society and Ra replayable, plus a genuine new skill (dial-reading) to master across plays.
ideas.producibility_notes: 6 part types. The tide dial is the single riskiest component in this set — two concentric rotating rings on one shared center axle is a more demanding joint than a single-ring dial (needs two independent friction fits at different diameters sharing one pivot pin), but it appears in only 1 instance in the entire game, which contains the risk to getting one part right rather than compounding it across many units. Player bid board cover flaps (5 instances, one per player) are simple hinge-or-slide covers, a low-tolerance-sensitivity feature even repeated 5 times. No feature is under 1mm.

ideas.title: Mancala: Solar Harvest
ideas.concept: The ancient two-player sowing game Mancala, restyled as a sleek space-station energy grid where you're sowing glowing energy orbs between collector nodes to fill your reactor core. The classic rules are untouched — the tension is exactly the counting-and-capturing puzzle Mancala players already know — but the board reads as a piece of hardware, not a farm.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Mancala/Kalah, the traditional 2-row, 6-pit sowing game (per search, BGG's Traditional Games: Mancala family lists 100+ variants, with Kalah as 'the most successful modern game' — an ancient, public-domain ruleset with no publisher IP to clear). This entry is a pure styling reskin: pits become 'collector nodes,' the two stores become 'reactor cores,' seeds become translucent glow-look 'energy orbs,' and the board is CAD-modeled as an angular space-dock rather than a wooden bowl-board — no rule, scoring, or turn-structure change from standard Kalah rules.
ideas.rules: 2 players, ages 6+, 15-20 min. SETUP: Place 4 energy orbs in each of the 12 collector nodes (6 per player, in the row nearest them); each player's reactor core (large end pit) starts empty. TURN: pick up all orbs from any one of your own non-empty collector nodes and sow them one at a time counterclockwise into each following node, including your own reactor core if you reach it, but skipping your opponent's reactor core entirely. If your very last orb lands in your own reactor core, take another turn immediately. If your last orb lands in a previously-empty node on your own side, and the node directly opposite (on your opponent's side) contains orbs, capture both your last orb and all orbs from the opposite node into your own reactor core. GAME END: when a player's entire row of collector nodes is empty at the start of their turn, the game ends; the other player immediately sweeps all remaining orbs on their own side into their own reactor core. WIN: the player with the most orbs in their reactor core wins.
ideas.components: 1 mancala board, PETG, molded as a space-station dock with 12 collector-node pits (6 per side) and 2 larger reactor-core end pits, 40x14cm x 3cm thick; 48 energy orb tokens, PLA (translucent glow-look finish), 1.5cm spheres; storage box, PETG, fitted to hold board and orbs.
ideas.demand_case: Mancala is one of the oldest and most continuously played board game families in the world, with BGG's Traditional Games: Mancala family listing over 100 documented variants and Kalah cited as its most successful modern commercial form, and the game is sold in wide retail distribution (Amazon, Walmart per search) confirming an enormous, evergreen mainstream audience for the base ruleset. Target audience: family game night and casual players, ages 6+, seeking a fast, deterministic, counting-based abstract game with broad multi-generational appeal.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is a well-proven, low-luck counting puzzle — Mancala's appeal comes from the near-perfect-information tactile satisfaction of tracking seed distribution and setting up captures, a design validated by centuries of continuous play and 100+ documented variants. A sci-fi hardware restyle doesn't touch that core loop, it simply gives an already-loved 15-20 min game a fresh, giftable visual identity for buyers who want the classic experience with a different look on the shelf.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 part types, zero moving joints, no fit tolerances beyond a pit deep enough to hold up to ~12+ spheres loosely (a solved, extremely low-risk FDM geometry). The only design consideration is keeping the reactor-core end pits large enough (recommend 6cm dia minimum) to visually hold up to 24+ captured orbs without overflowing during endgame play.

ideas.title: Nine Men's Morris: Ghost Manor
ideas.concept: The ancient two-player strategy game Nine Men's Morris, restyled as a haunted mansion where translucent ghost pieces try to escape capture by lantern-wielding hunter pieces across the mansion's hallway grid. The classic mill-forming, piece-removing rules are completely unchanged — only the visual world around them has shifted from abstract lines to a spooky floor plan.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Nine Men's Morris, an ancient (Roman-era) public-domain 2-player abstract strategy game with an active BGG presence (multiple listed editions including 'Nine Men's Morris Evolution') and continuous commercial retail sale in wood editions (e.g. WE Games per search) — no publisher IP to clear. This entry is a pure styling reskin: the classic 24-point three-concentric-square grid is worked into a haunted-mansion floor-plan artwork, and the two piece sets become translucent 'ghosts' and opaque 'hunters' — no change to placement phase, movement phase, mill-formation, or capture rules from the standard ruleset.
ideas.rules: 2 players, ages 8+, 20-30 min. SETUP: The board shows the classic 24-point grid (three concentric squares connected by midpoint lines) worked into a mansion hallway floor plan. Each player takes 9 pieces (one player takes translucent ghost pieces, the other opaque hunter pieces); the board starts empty. PHASE 1 (Placing): players alternate turns placing one of their pieces on any empty point on the board. If placing a piece completes a 'mill' (three of your own pieces in a row along one of the board's marked lines), you immediately remove one opponent piece of your choice that is NOT currently part of one of their own mills (if all opponent pieces are in mills, you may remove any one). Continue until both players have placed all 9 pieces. PHASE 2 (Moving): players alternate turns sliding one of their own pieces along a marked line to an adjacent empty point (no jumping). Forming a mill this way (including breaking a mill and re-forming it later by moving out and back) again triggers the same removal rule as Phase 1. WIN: reduce your opponent to only 2 remaining pieces, or trap your opponent so they have no legal move on their turn — either condition ends the game immediately in your favor.
ideas.components: 1 manor board, PETG, 30x30cm, printed with the classic 24-point three-concentric-square morris grid worked into a haunted mansion hallway floor-plan design; 9 ghost pieces, PLA (translucent finish), 2.5cm pawn-shaped minis; 9 hunter pieces, PLA (opaque, lantern-holding sculpt), 2.5cm pawn-shaped minis; storage box, PETG.
ideas.demand_case: Nine Men's Morris is a documented ancient game (dating to at least the Roman Empire per Wikipedia/search) with an established BGG listing, multiple modern editions, and continuous mainstream retail sale (WE Games wooden travel edition on Amazon per search), confirming a durable, broad classic-abstract-strategy audience across generations. Target audience: family game night and classic-abstract-game collectors, ages 8+, who enjoy solved-but-satisfying strategy games like checkers or tic-tac-toe's deeper cousins.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision each turn is mill-formation tempo and blocking — deciding whether to build toward your own three-in-a-row or spend a move denying your opponent's near-complete line, a tight tactical puzzle that has kept Nine Men's Morris played and taught for roughly two thousand years per its documented history. The haunted-mansion theme gives the abstract grid a narrative hook (ghosts evading capture by hunters) that makes the classic ruleset more approachable and giftable to the stated family audience without touching the proven game underneath.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 part types, zero moving joints or assembly hardware, no fit tolerances beyond pieces resting on flat board points (a fully solved, extremely low-risk FDM geometry). The only design consideration is keeping the grid line engraving on the board crisp enough (recommend 1.5-2mm groove width) to clearly show legal movement paths during Phase 2, well above the under-1mm risk threshold.
